cards.what_happened: LAUGFS cooking gas cylinder prices have been cut after the Ministry of Trade intervened. A 12.5kg cylinder drops by Rs. 745, from Rs. 6,740 to Rs. 5,995. A 5kg cylinder falls by Rs. 322, from Rs. 2,720 to Rs. 2,398.
details: Minister of Trade Wasantha Samarasinghe announced that LAUGFS gas cylinder prices have been reduced. He said the cuts were made after the Ministry of Trade intervened.
A 12.5kg cylinder now costs Rs. 5,995, down from Rs. 6,740, a reduction of Rs. 745. A 5kg cylinder falls from Rs. 2,720 to Rs. 2,398, a reduction of Rs. 322.
According to the Minister, the revised prices provide relief to consumers purchasing LAUGFS domestic cooking gas cylinders.
cards.why_it_matters: The lower prices give relief to consumers who buy LAUGFS domestic cooking gas cylinders.

12.5kg cylinder drops Rs. 745, from Rs. 6,740 to Rs. 5,995.
5kg cylinder drops Rs. 322, from Rs. 2,720 to Rs. 2,398.
Trade Minister Wasantha Samarasinghe announced the revised prices.
Lower prices bring relief to consumers buying LAUGFS cooking gas.
cards.blurb: LAUGFS gas cylinders are cheaper: a 12.5kg cylinder drops Rs. 745 after Ministry of Trade intervention.
cards.spoken: Good news for households that cook with LAUGFS gas. The Ministry of Trade stepped in, and the price of a 12.5kg LAUGFS cylinder has come down by Rs. 745, from Rs. 6,740 to Rs. 5,995. The smaller 5kg cylinder is also cheaper, falling by Rs. 322, from Rs. 2,720 to Rs. 2,398. Minister of Trade Wasantha Samarasinghe announced the new prices and said the cuts followed the ministry's intervention. He added that the revised prices bring relief to consumers who buy LAUGFS domestic cooking gas cylinders. So for anyone filling LAUGFS gas at home, the new prices mean paying less than before.

world.title: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?

cards.what_happened: Donald Trump will attend the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, this week and is expected to meet Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin. The talks are expected to focus on AI regulation, trade and Taiwan, with little chance of major breakthroughs. The summit follows Democrats winning control of Congress and comes amid scrutiny over Jensen Huang and alleged spy Alice Huang.
details: Donald Trump, the United States president, will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where 21 Pacific Rim member economies are taking part. He is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and to hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines would be the third time the two leaders have met this year, after Xi hosted Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September, with earlier meetings heavy on ceremony, aimed at showing stability in a consequential relationship, and light on meaningful breakthroughs.

Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, with AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan likely to loom large. The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on Trump in his final two years, while Beijing is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next. Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi but the meeting is unlikely to produce substantive breakthroughs, Yury Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy adviser, told reporters on Monday that the significance and symbolism of the meetings between the three superpower leaders are hard to overestimate, neither side has released a formal agenda for the expected Trump-Xi meeting, and the White House said the countries will support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December and agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.

AI regulation is set to loom large, with the US and China, as industry leaders, facing pressure to jointly agree safeguards on the transformative technology, after both sides pledged in September to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and hold a dialogue on emerging risks. The Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails, Trump said after the White House meeting that the US would not be putting on brakes on the AI industry, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, said both sides expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology, while adding that they should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China and that their approach to every challenge will not always converge. The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting even if it is not directly addressed, because Huang's close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing; Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China, and Crisis Group's Wyne said Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts; some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart, and Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement; the Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi, and China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.

Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi. Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, in great detail with the Chinese president, even though the US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act and, under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales. In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump referred to Taiwan as a very good negotiating chip with China and has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island, while Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of the German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote that the language invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval and that the more successful the bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it and treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act; the White House defended the delay by citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, and the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce, and Democratic control of Congress plus general bipartisan support for Taiwan could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump's final two years.
cards.why_it_matters: The article calls the US-China relationship consequential and says the summit follows Democrats winning control of Congress, a likely check on Trump.
key_facts: Trump will attend APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, with 21 Pacific Rim economies.
He is expected to meet Xi Jinping and hold three-way meeting with Putin.
Trump-Xi meeting would be third this year after Beijing in May and White House in September.
Experts expect ceremony, not breakthroughs; AI, trade and Taiwan loom.
Democrats won both chambers of Congress, likely checking Trump; Beijing looks beyond him.
White House says countries agreed to strategic stability based on respect, fairness, reciprocity.
Jensen Huang resignation, alleged spy Alice Huang, and Lutnick scrutiny loom over talks.
Trump held up $14bn Taiwan arms package, citing production limits and trade truce.
cards.whats_next: No formal agenda has been released, but Trump will attend the APEC summit this week and is expected to meet Xi and Putin; the White House says the countries will support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
cards.blurb: Trump heads to Shenzhen for APEC talks with Xi and Putin as AI, trade, Taiwan and an alleged spy scandal loom.
cards.spoken: President Donald Trump is heading to Shenzhen, China, this week for the APEC summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim economies, where he is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and also hold a three way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. It would be Trump and Xi's third meeting this year, after Beijing in May and the White House in September, but experts expect more ceremony than breakthroughs. AI regulation, trade and Taiwan are likely to dominate, along with the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and questions about alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang. The talks come just after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, adding pressure on Trump. The White House says the two countries agreed to build strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, and will support each other at APEC and the G20 summit in Florida in December.

world.title: White House withdraws nomination of Heidi Overton to lead FDA

cards.what_happened: The White House withdrew Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA a day before a Senate health committee vote. Overton, a physician and abortion opponent with strong Trump ties, faced bipartisan concerns over her stance on vaccines and scientific independence. Reproductive rights groups celebrated the withdrawal, warning about future anti‑abortion nominees.
details: The White House dropped Overton’s nomination after Trump nominated her in August. Overton, a physician and prominent abortion opponent, has spent most of her career working for Trump or conservative groups. Her nomination was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the agency after a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Marty Makary.

Overton faced bipartisan Senate questions about her willingness to break from Trump, especially his unsupported claims about childhood vaccine dangers. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, remained undecided ahead of Wednesday’s committee vote. Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for breaking up combination vaccines “almost disqualifying” and pressed her on scientific independence during a September hearing.

A reproductive rights group praised the withdrawal. Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, said Overton posed a serious threat to medication abortion access and warned about future nominees. Overton’s 2023 policy brief urged strict regulation of the abortion pill mifeprestone and criticized mailing of abortion pills. To be confirmed, Overton would have needed all 12 Republican votes on the committee; Democrats hold 11 seats. Republicans are racing to confirm Trump’s remaining nominees before the Senate Democrats take power in January.

cards.blurb: The White House withdrew physician Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination amid Senate concerns over vaccines and abortion rights.
cards.spoken: Here’s what’s happening on the political scene today. The White House has pulled the plug on Dr. Heidi Overton’s bid to lead the Food and Drug Administration, just one day before a crucial vote in the Senate health committee. Overton, a physician who has long opposed abortion and has ties to former President Trump’s inner circle, faced tough questions from lawmakers about her independence, especially regarding Trump’s claims about childhood vaccines. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the committee, says he’s still undecided, having previously called her support for breaking up combination vaccines “almost disqualifying.” Reproductive rights groups are cheering the withdrawal, warning that another anti‑abortion nominee could threaten medication abortion access. Meanwhile, Republicans are racing to confirm the rest of Trump’s nominees before the new Congress takes over in January.
